q: The combined equation ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0 represents:
o: A pair of lines through the origin
why: A homogeneous second-degree equation in x, y represents a pair of straight lines through the origin.

q: The pair of lines ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0 are real and distinct when:
why: Lines are real and distinct when h^2 > ab, i.e., h^2 - ab > 0.

q: The two lines represented by ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0 are coincident when:
why: Coincident lines occur when the discriminant condition h^2 - ab = 0.

The pair of lines ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0 are perpendicular to each other when:
why: Lines are perpendicular when the sum of coefficients of x^2 and y^2 is zero, i.e., a+b = 0.

q: The pair of lines represented by ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0 are coincident (parallel, same line) when, in addition to h^2 = ab:
o: a and b must be negative
why: Since the homogeneous equation always passes through the origin, coincident lines also pass through origin.

q: The general second-degree equation ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 represents a pair of straight lines when:
why: This is the standard determinant condition for the general second-degree equation to represent a pair of lines.

q: To separate the two lines from ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0, we treat the equation as quadratic in:
why: Dividing by x^2 or y^2 gives a quadratic in the ratio y/x (or x/y) which factors into two linear equations.

q: For the pair of lines x^2 - y^2 = 0, the two separate lines are:
why: x^2 - y^2 = (x-y)(x+y) = 0 gives lines x = y and x = -y.

q: If the lines represented by ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0 are parallel to each other (i.e. they coincide), the single line obtained is given by:
why: When h^2 = ab, the pair reduces to the repeated line sqrt(a)x + sqrt(b)y = 0, consistent with ax + hy = 0 form.
